summary: Defines PANA, a network-layer transport for EAP that lets clients authenticate to an access network. In EAP terms it is a UDP-based lower layer between the EAP peer and the authenticator. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Before using a school network you must show your pass. PANA carries that proof over the network itself, even without special wires.

questions: eap over udp for network access
protocol for carrying authentication for network access
what are the phases of a pana session
subtitle: A UDP-based way to carry EAP authentication between a client and an access network, whatever the link layer.

tldr.problem: Networks need to authenticate and authorize clients before giving them access, and a protocol is needed to carry authentication methods between the client and the access network over any link technology.
tldr.mechanism: PANA carries EAP messages inside its own UDP-based requests and answers (port 716), with sequence numbers, retransmission and optional per-message integrity protection derived from the EAP key.
tldr.outcome: Any EAP method can be used for network access above IP. RFC 5191 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5872.

today: RFC 5191 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5872. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: A Transport for Network Access Authentication
sections.content:
Secure network access needs access control based on authenticating and authorizing clients. PANA is a network-layer transport for the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). In EAP terms it is a UDP-based EAP lower layer between the EAP peer and the EAP authenticator. Because EAP rides above IP, any method that can be carried as an EAP method becomes available to PANA and to any link-layer technology.

Several pieces of a full solution are outside this RFC: discovery of the PANA Authentication Agent, authentication method choice, the protocol between the agent and the enforcement point, access control filter creation and data traffic protection. They are covered in RFC 5193 and RFC 5192.
sections.eli5: PANA is the delivery truck for the proof of who you are. What the proof looks like is decided elsewhere.

sections.title: The Players and Sessions
sections.content:
The PANA Client (PaC) sits in the access device with the EAP peer and provides credentials. The PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) in the access network verifies them and authorizes access. It sits with the EAP authenticator and may offload the work to a back end AAA infrastructure. An Enforcement Point (EP) applies per-packet filters and should block data traffic from unauthorized clients, except PANA and a few allowed types such as ARP, IPv6 neighbor discovery and DHCP.

A PANA session links one PaC and one PAA. It has a fixed session identifier, assigned by the PAA, and cannot be shared across network interfaces. It ends on an authentication or liveness failure, retransmissions running out, lifetime expiry, an explicit termination message or any event that ends the access service.
sections.eli5: You are the visitor, the PAA is the front desk, and the enforcement point is the door guard who only lets you in once the front desk agrees.

sections.title: The Four Phases
sections.content:
A session has four phases. In authentication and authorization, either side starts the session: the PaC sends a PANA-Client-Initiation, or the PAA sends an unsolicited PANA-Auth-Request. EAP messages travel in Auth-Requests, and Auth-Answers mostly acknowledge them, though an answer MAY piggyback an EAP message. The first pair carries the 'S' (Start) bit and the last pair the 'C' (Complete) bit, and the final request carries the result.

In the access phase the client uses the network, and either side may send a ping (a Notification with the 'P' bit) to test liveness. Implementations MUST limit the rate of this test. In re-authentication, EAP runs again to extend the session lifetime, started by the PaC (a Notification with the 'A' bit) or by the PAA, which MUST start before the lifetime expires. In the termination phase, either side sends a PANA-Termination-Request and, on a valid acknowledgment, all session state is removed immediately.

If the PAA wants to stay stateless on a PANA-Client-Initiation, it leaves out the EAP-Payload AVP in its first request and does not retransmit it, so the PaC MUST keep retransmitting until it gets the second request. If both sides start at once, the PAA MUST silently discard the PaC's initiation.
sections.eli5: First you show your pass and get in. While inside, the guard may ask "are you still there?" Sometimes you must show your pass again, and at the end you say goodbye.

sections.title: Messages and AVPs
sections.content:
PANA runs over UDP, unicast between the PaC and PAA. The assigned well-known port is 716, and all peers MUST listen on it. The header has a 16-bit Reserved field, Message Length, 16-bit Flags, Message Type, a 32-bit Session Identifier and a 32-bit Sequence Number, followed by AVPs. The flags are R (request), S (start), C (complete), A (re-authentication), P (ping) and I (IP reconfiguration).

There are seven messages in four types: Client-Initiation (1), Auth Request and Answer (2), Termination Request and Answer (3) and Notification Request and Answer (4). Information travels in AVPs (attribute-value pairs), with codes 1 to 9: AUTH, EAP-Payload, Integrity-Algorithm, Key-Id, Nonce, PRF-Algorithm, Result-Code, Session-Lifetime and Termination-Cause.

Result-Code is 0 for success, 1 when authentication is rejected and 2 when authorization is rejected even though authentication succeeded. The Session-Lifetime AVP counts seconds remaining before the session expires.
sections.eli5: Every PANA note has a header with who and what it is, and labeled slots for extras such as the proof, a secret number or how long you may stay.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Retransmission
sections.content:
PANA gives ordered, reliable delivery on top of UDP. Each side keeps a 32-bit counter for its next outgoing request and one for the next expected incoming request. The counters go up by 1 per request and wrap to zero after 2^32-1. Initial values are picked at random, and the PANA-Client-Initiation carries sequence number 0. An answer repeats its request's number, and a peer may have only one outstanding request at a time.

Requests are retransmitted on a timer modelled on DHCPv6. The first timeout is IRT plus a random factor between -0.1 and +0.1, and later timeouts roughly double, capped by MRT. The defaults for requests are 1 second initial, 30 seconds maximum and 10 retransmissions, after which the session MUST be terminated. The client-initiation uses 1 second initial and 120 seconds maximum, with no retry limit. Duplicate requests MUST be answered (unless rate limited), and the last answer MAY be cached.

PANA has no fragmentation of its own and relies on EAP methods and IP.
sections.eli5: Each note is numbered so nothing arrives out of order. If you hear nothing back, you ask again after waiting a little longer each time, and give up after ten tries.

sections.title: Keys and Message Protection
sections.content:
If the EAP method makes a Master Session Key (MSK), PANA builds a PANA security association from it. The PANA_AUTH_KEY is derived with the prf+ function from the MSK, the string "IETF PANA", the initial request and answer, both nonces and the Key-Id. The AUTH AVP then carries a message authentication code over the whole message. The PRF and integrity algorithm are negotiated in the first request and answer, and all implementations MUST support PRF_HMAC_SHA1 (2) and AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 (7).

Nonces MUST be 8 to 256 octets, and the maximum SHOULD be 20 octets. Each new MSK gets a new Key-Id and new keys, and the SA lives as long as the session. Once an MSK exists, the request carrying EAP Success and every later message MUST carry a valid AUTH AVP.

Invalid messages MUST be discarded to resist denial of service attacks. If the PaC's IP address changes, it MUST send any valid PANA message so the PAA can update the session.
sections.eli5: Once you have shown your pass, you and the front desk make a secret handshake. Every note after that carries it, so nobody can slip in fake notes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sequence numbers, randomly initialized, make it harder to spoof messages unless the attacker can eavesdrop, and stale messages are discarded. When the EAP method generates keys, the AUTH AVP stops man-in-the-middle attacks, injection, replay and modification. In networks whose lower layers are already secure, cryptographic protection of PANA messages is not necessary.

The initial exchange is not authenticated and is open to spoofing, so the PAA should create as little state as possible in response to PANA-Client-Initiation messages. Weak EAP methods can expose users to dictionary or replay attacks, and the optional EAP Response/Identity can reveal identity. Operators and users are responsible for choosing a proper EAP method. Periodic keep-alive pinging may cause congestion and false alarms.
sections.eli5: The very first hello can be faked, so the front desk keeps it simple and does not remember much until the real checking starts.
